newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK future leader reappoints top colonial team.
newsitem.headline: HK future leader reappoints top colonial team.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa chose continuity and announced on Thursday he would re-appoint the territory's top tier of civil servants to their positions in his post-colonial administration.

Hong Kong's popular and influential Chief Secretary Anson Chan, deputy to departing British Governor Chris Patten, will serve as Tung's number two when Hong Kong reverts to China later this year. Her post will be renamed Administrative Secretary.
Financial Secretary Donald Tsang would also remain in his position as Hong Kong's top economic policy planner, a decision likely to be welcomed by the markets.

"My principal consideration is, firstly, that they are good, and secondly, that it is most important during the transition we (have) as minimum changes as possible," Tung told reporters upon his return from Beijing where he won approval for his list.
More than 150 years of British rule ends at midnight on June 30, 1997, now 131 days away.
Prominent lawyer Elsie Leung was named as secretary for justice, replacing Attorney General Jeremy Mathews who, as a non-ethnic Chinese, was not eligible to remain in his position.
"Miss Leung is highly respected in the legal profession as a liberal and fair-minded person with a strong sense of integrity and commitment to Hong Kong," Tung said.
Tung had flown to Beijing to report on his decision to China's top leadership, landing in the Chinese capital just hours before the announcement of the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Tung, a Shanghai-born shipping magnate, was selected in December to succeed Patten when British rule of Hong Kong ends.
One key position not yet chosen was that of chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's de facto central bank. It is currently held by Joseph Yam.
While important, the head of the HKMA is currently chosen by the Financial Secretary, not the territory's leader, and does not need to be ratified by China.
There had been speculation Tung would have the HKMA report directly to him and would name its chief on Thursday.
"I would like to review this matter in the future together with the Financial Secretary and the Chief Secreatry as we move forward," he told reporters on Thursday.
An HKMA spokesman said the situation remained unchanged and that Yam continued to report to the Financial Secretary.
In a statement, Patten said he welcomed the reappointments of key officials to the post-handover government.

"I have been most fortunate during my time as governor to be supported by an outstanding civil service, and I am pleased that Mr Tung Chee Hwa will continue to be served by an excellent team of senior officials," Patten said.
Tung won widespread public acclaim last month when he invited Chan to remain in her post. Many had feared her ties with the outgoing British would scupper her chances.
Tung said last month he would follow the practice of the outgoing colonial administration of reserving slots for the top three civil servants on his Executive Council, or inner cabinet.

He also named two members of Patten's inner circle to his executive council last month, a move seen as likely to minimise the inevitable disruption resulting from what will be a monumental change for Hong Kong.

Academic Michael DeGolyer, director of the long-term 1997 transition project studying the handover, said it was a wise decision to limit the degree of change in the sensitive countdown to the handover and following Deng's death.
"I think then it becomes even more important for Tung Chee-hwa to do reassuring things, such as ensuring continuity of the civil service," DeGolyer said.
